Q: What should I put to distro conf and what to image recipe? A:

Use this rule of thumb:

  • distro.conf = policy shared by all images of that distro

    Put here things like:

    • DISTRO_FEATURES

    • init system choice (systemd vs sysvinit)

    • package format / package manager policy

    • security / debug / licensing / provider defaults

    • global PREFERRED_PROVIDER, VIRTUAL-RUNTIME_*, PACKAGE_CLASSES, etc.

  • image recipe (*.bb) = contents of one concrete image

    Put here things like:

    • IMAGE_INSTALL

    • IMAGE_FEATURES

    • extra users, packages, tools

    • whether this image is dev, production, rescue, minimal, etc.

A good test:

  • If changing it should affect every image built for that distro → put it in distro.conf

  • If changing it should affect only one image variant → put it in the image recipe

Example:

# distro.conf
DISTRO_FEATURES:append = " systemd wifi"
VIRTUAL-RUNTIME_init_manager = "systemd"
PACKAGE_CLASSES = "package_ipk"

# dev-image.bb
IMAGE_FEATURES += " ssh-server-openssh debug-tweaks"
IMAGE_INSTALL += " gdb strace vim"

So in your case:

  • dev.conf / user.conf should describe system-wide distro policy

  • dev-image.bb / user-image.bb should describe what packages/features each image contains

Q: C++ Error "Variable-sized object may not be initialized A:

The error implies that nodes is not a compile time constant which is a requirement for defining arrays in standard C++. A valid C++ example:

constexpr std::size_t nodes = 10;
bool visited[nodes]{};

There is also some differences between the two arrays.

Had variable length arrays been valid C++, this would define an array of nodes amount of vector<bool>s. Each vector<bool> could then grow and shrink dynamically (if this is std::vector and not some other kind of vector):

vector<bool> visited[nodes] = {0};

This would define an array of bools (again, had variable length arrays been valid C++):

bool visited[nodes] = {0};

Variable length arrays is however not standard C++. They exist in C, but not even in C can you use an initializer. Well, since C23 you can, but it has to be empty:

bool visited[nodes] = {};

In C++, you'd use one the std::vector constructor taking a count to initialize it to hold the number of bools you want:

std::vector<bool> visited(nodes);        // nodes number of default-inserted (false) bools
std::vector<bool> visited(nodes, false); // nodes number of copy constructed bools

Some C++ implementations do accept variable length arrays as an extension and some even accept them with an initializer:

bool visited[nodes] = {false}; // accepted by gcc as an extension

I suggest that you learn to use the standard C++ containers, like std::vector instead.

Be aware though: std::vector<bool> is often specialized to occupy as little memory as possible. That means it will pack the bools with as many it can fit in a byte. That means, it usually fits 8 bools in one byte (but on some platforms even more). This makes it a bit odd to work with and a bit slower than one would expect in some situations.

Q: Any Potential Issues With Struct A Being Referenced in Struct B and Vice Versa? A:

There's no inherent problem with One and Two each holding a pointer to the other.

And the code you posted (assigning all fields and then accessing one->two_ptr->one_ptr-> ...) - has no UB.

However this pattern requires you to carefully manage the allocation/initialization and deallocations, to avoid using dangling-pointers (which is invoking UB).

A side note:
Next time please post such a question as a "normal" (newly AKA Troubleshooting/Debugging) question rather than an open-ended "advice" one. It should have some clear answer(s), and does not seem opinion-based.

Q: Determine the line of code that causes a segmentation fault? A:

GCC can't do that but GDB (a debugger) sure can. Compile your program using the -g switch, like this:

gcc program.c -g

Then use gdb:

$ gdb ./a.out
(gdb) run
<segfault happens here>
(gdb) backtrace
<offending code is shown here>

Here is a nice tutorial to get you started with GDB.

Where the segfault occurs is generally only a clue as to where "the mistake which causes" it is in the code. The given location is not necessarily where the problem resides.
